results.title: Necessity of Embase, Scopus and Web of Science as database for systematic review? | ResearchGate
results.content: Published Time: Mon, 05 May 25 07:36:16 +0000 Necessity of Embase, Scopus and Web of Science as database for systematic review? Necessity of Embase, Scopus and Web of Science as database for systematic review? I want to enquire if Embase, Scopus and Web of Science are mandatory for a systematic review? Optimal database combinations for literature searches in systematic reviews: a prospective exploratory study Zhen Yu Wong Top contributors to discussions in this field Learn how to best influence lab equipment purchasing behavior **Get help with your research** Join ResearchGate to ask questions, get input, and advance your work. In my view, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science are not mandatory for a systematic review. But Pubmed/Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar and Cochrane are commonly used databases for systematic reviews. The customary "Big 3" databases for systematic review are PubMed (which includes MEDLINE), EMBASE and the Cochrane Library (which includes the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials or CENTRAL). As for Scopus and Web of Science (which I think are also subscription-based), I have yet to see recent evidence that these databases have already reached the level of importance of PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library and EMBASE in terms of indexed literature content. results.content: Add your text between the p tags. # Literature Search Guide. Learn how to search for articles in databases. ## Search in Medline or Embase in Ovid. * Embase *This link opens in a new window*. An international (and European focused) biomedical and pharmacological database that provides access to up-to-date information about medical, allied health, and drug-related subjects. * Medline (Ovid) *This link opens in a new window*. Medline is the major database for finding journal articles in the fields of medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine, nursing, pre-clinical sciences and the health care system. Ovid's version provides direct full text for ~300 journals (with no embargo period), but will connect to all the full text available from the combined e-HLbc resources. Ovid Medline also links to the full text from the EBMR databases. * Introduction to Embase on OVID (Wolters Kluwer). This course highlights the unique structure of this database (including Emtree and the Thesaurus) and includes a detailed review of specific limits, fields and search tips for this resource. * Introducing the Embase Advanced Techniques on Ovid (Wolters Kluwer). Learn more about searching using Emtree, floating subheadings, and implementing specific limits such as clinical queries, MEDLINE, Publication types and conference materials. * OVID Advanced Search (Wolters Kluwer). This video demonstrates the advanced search features in Ovid. It uses Medline database as an exmaple. ## Search in EBSCO Medline. Medline can also be searched in EBSCO. This is great for quick and simply keyword searching. For more comprehensive searches, we recommend using the Ovid interface. * Medline with Full Text (EBSCO) *This link opens in a new window*. Medline is the major database for finding journal articles in the fields of medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine, nursing, pre-clinical sciences and the health care system. EBSCO's version includes full text for ~1400 journals and will connect to all the full text available from the combined e-HLbc resources. Many journals are subject to embargo periods ranging from 3-18 months after publication before the full text is made available in the database. Ready to try the new Medline user interface? Use the Search feature to find videos on Medline. * Medline with Full Text Take-Away Guide.

Title: Embase - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
The search strategy was developed without any language restriction and run on www.embase.com. We supplemented our search by manually reviewing the reference list of all retrieved articles. ### Databases and search strategy. Studies published between 1st January 2010 and 4th July 2022 were searched from Embase, PubMed, African Journals Online and Google Scholar. The search terms used were similar to those by previous similar systematic reviews [5,19]. The search was conducted using Embase subject headings (Emtree) and medical subject headings (MeSH) in Embase and PubMed, respectively (Supplementary Data). No restrictions in study design and language were applied in the search and cited references were reviewed to identify additional studies. Two bibliographic databases (OVID-Medline, Embase Classic + Embase) were searched for published, peer-reviewed, literature, and one repository (Medrxiv) were searched to identify pre-print records on January 28th, 2021. Three electronic databases (Medline, Embase and EMCare) were searched for any articles published until January 2022. Reference lists of identified articles were scanned for additional studies, and forward reference searching (identifying articles which cite relevant articles) was performed. Embase Ovid and MEDLINE Ovid databases, along with the National Health Service Economic Evaluation database (NHS EED), were searched on 5th April 2017 to identify articles that:. When searching Embase and MEDLINE, terms from both components were used (Appendix 1, see online supplementary material); searching the NHS EED database, which only includes health economic studies, did not require economic modelling terms. Searches were restricted to articles published in the English language. The Embase/MEDLINE search was updated on 4th June 2020 to identify any recently published work. The following electronic databases were systematically searched: EMBASE, MEDLINE, CINAHL, WHOLIS, and Web of Science from January 1999 to April 2016. A comprehensive search strategy was developed for EMBASE (Supplementary Appendix A) and subsequently adjusted as required to suit other databases. The reference lists of all eligible articles were manually searched to identify other eligible studies. Databases of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched through 2015 Feb. with no restriction to regions or languages. The reference lists of the initially identified articles and systemic review articles were manually searched.
